title: The Lesson I Learned From Matthew
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Matthew
The Man Everyone Wrote Off... Until Jesus Rewrote His Story
There are moments in life when you become painfully aware of how people see you.
Not who you truly are.
Not who God created you to be.
But who they have decided you are.
Maybe it was one mistake.
One failure.
One addiction.
One relationship.
One season of compromise.
One scandal.
And suddenly your entire identity became attached to your worst chapter.
People stopped seeing your heart.
They only remembered your history.
If you've ever felt that way, then the story of Matthew may be one of the most important stories you will ever read.
Because Matthew's story is not simply about a tax collector.
It is about every person who thinks they have gone too far.
Every person carrying shame.
Every person trapped by labels.
Every person who secretly wonders if God could still use someone like them.
The Gospel introduces Matthew with remarkable simplicity.
Matthew 9:9 says:
"As Jesus passed on from there, He saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and He said to him, 'Follow Me.' And he rose and followed Him."
The verse feels almost too short.
Too simple.
Too easy.
But hidden inside those few words is one of the most shocking moments in Scripture.
Matthew was not respected.
He was despised.
Tax collectors in first-century Judea were often viewed as traitors who worked for the Roman Empire. Many were known for corruption and exploitation. They represented greed, compromise, and betrayal.
To the religious community, Matthew was exactly the kind of person who should never be considered spiritual leadership material.
Yet Jesus walked directly toward him.
Not away from him.
The original Greek text records Jesus saying:
"ἀκολούθει μοι" (akolouthei moi)
"Follow Me."
This was not merely an invitation.
It was a call to a completely new identity.

The Greek word "ἀκολουθέω" (akoloutheō) means more than physically walking behind someone. It carries the idea of attaching oneself to another, becoming a disciple, sharing their way of life, and embracing their mission.
Jesus was not inviting Matthew into religion.
Jesus was inviting Matthew into transformation.
And Matthew got up immediately.
He left the booth.
He left the money.
He left the security.
He left the old life.
Because when Jesus reveals who He is, the things we once clung to suddenly lose their power.
But the story becomes even more beautiful.
Jesus didn't simply save Matthew.
He sat at Matthew's table.
Matthew 9:10 tells us that many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Jesus.
The religious leaders were scandalized.
How could a rabbi sit among people like this?
How could someone claiming holiness associate with the morally broken?
The answer reveals the very heart of the Gospel.
Jesus replied:
"It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick."
Then He added:
"I desire mercy, not sacrifice."
Those words come directly from the Hebrew Scriptures.
Jesus was quoting Hosea 6:6.
In Hebrew, God says:
"כִּי חֶסֶד חָפַצְתִּי וְלֹא זָבַח"
(Ki chesed chafatzti velo zavach)
"For I desire mercy and not sacrifice."
The word "חֶסֶד" (chesed) is one of the richest words in the entire Old Testament.
It speaks of covenant love.
Steadfast love.
Faithful love.
Merciful love.
The kind of love God continues to show people even when they do not deserve it.
Jesus was reminding everyone that God has always been more interested in redeeming sinners than applauding self-righteous people.
That truth still confronts us today.
Because many people secretly believe they need to clean themselves up before coming to Christ.
They think they need to become worthy first.
Less broken.
Less sinful.
Less damaged.
Less complicated.
But Matthew's story destroys that lie.
Jesus did not wait for Matthew to change.
Jesus called Matthew while he was still sitting in the tax booth.
Jesus met him in the middle of the scandal.
In the middle of the compromise.
In the middle of the mess.
Because grace does not begin after transformation.
Grace is what makes transformation possible.
Perhaps that is why Matthew's Gospel carries such power.
Every chapter feels like the testimony of a man who never got over being chosen.
Imagine writing the very Gospel that would be read by billions throughout history.
Imagine becoming one of the twelve apostles.
Imagine being entrusted with recording the teachings of the Son of God.
None of that seemed possible when Matthew was sitting at his tax booth.
Yet Jesus saw what nobody else could see.
While others saw a scandal, Jesus saw a disciple.
While others saw corruption, Jesus saw purpose.
While others saw failure, Jesus saw redemption.
While others saw a dead end, Jesus saw a future.
And maybe that is exactly what you need to hear today.
The enemy constantly reminds people of their past.
Jesus constantly points people toward their future.
The enemy says your failures define you.
Jesus says His grace defines you.
The enemy says your story is over.
Jesus says He is still writing.
The name "Jesus" comes from the Hebrew-Aramaic form:
"יֵשׁוּעַ" (Yeshua)
Meaning:
"The LORD saves."
Not the LORD condemns.
Not the LORD shames.
Not the LORD humiliates.
The LORD saves.
That is who Jesus has always been.
That is who Jesus remains today.
Maybe your tax booth looks different.
Maybe it is hidden bitterness.
Maybe it is addiction.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is fear.
Maybe it is anxiety.
Maybe it is regret.
Maybe it is a secret nobody knows about.
Whatever it is, Jesus still walks toward people sitting in places they never imagined they could leave.
And He still says:
"Follow Me."
The question is not whether Jesus is calling.
The question is whether we are willing to rise and follow.
Matthew's life stands as permanent evidence that God specializes in rewriting stories.
Not because people deserve it.
But because grace is bigger than scandal.
Because mercy is stronger than shame.
Because forgiveness reaches deeper than failure.
Because the Cross accomplished what human effort never could.
The Gospel is not the story of good people earning God's acceptance.
The Gospel is the story of a holy God rescuing undeserving people through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
That includes Matthew.
That includes me.
That includes you.
And that is why Matthew's story continues to captivate hearts more than two thousand years later.
We see ourselves in him.
We recognize the labels.
We recognize the failures.
We recognize the shame.
But we also recognize the hope.
Because if Jesus could transform Matthew, He can transform anyone.
Including us.
Maybe that's why this story is so difficult to forget.
Because deep down, every human heart longs for someone who can see beyond the worst thing we've ever done.
Someone who can look through the scandal and discover the soul beneath it.
Someone who can rewrite what everyone else assumed was final.
That Someone is Jesus Christ.
If this article spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What "tax booth" has Jesus been calling you to leave behind?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Not because salvation can be purchased—it cannot.
Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9).
But throughout Scripture, God's people supported the work of ministry so that the Gospel could continue reaching others (Philippians 4:15-18).
Because every share expands the reach of the Gospel.
Every testimony encourages another soul.
And every transformed life brings glory to Jesus Christ.
The greatest scandal was never Matthew's past.
The greatest scandal was that God's grace was greater than it.
